indicators.note: with its top cut off, the word for the garment loses its first letter

parts.note: a smock is a loose dress or overgarment

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a revealing outfit with no top half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' takes the S off SMOCK.
explanation.definitionFit: To mock is to ridicule or tease, a direct synonym of making fun of someone.

clue.text: Spaniel inanely nimble after inhaling helium

indicators.note: the jumbled word takes in the chemical symbol, as a lung would breathe in gas
done inanely, without sense, so the letters of nimble are jumbled

parts.note: He is the chemical symbol for helium

explanation.surface: A dog acts silly and sprightly after sucking on a party balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inanely' rearranges the letters of 'nimble' to BLENIM, and 'after inhaling' sets the gas symbol inside after the fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blenheim is a red-and-white variety of King Charles spaniel, named after the Marlborough palace.

clue.text: Nervously ran and hid round a corner initially, seeing this?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the other two, enclosing them
acting nervously, the letters of ran and hid get flustered and rearranged
only the starting letter of corner is used

explanation.surface: Someone panics and hides round a corner on spotting something scary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nervously' jumbles the two verbs to ARHNID, and 'round' wraps it about AC. The whole clue doubles as an arachnophobe's reaction, with 'seeing this?' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is the classic sight that makes a frightened person run and hide, and spiders belong to the arachnid class.

clue.text: Be employed one of two weekends

indicators.note: links the single choice to the pair it is made from, placing the choosing word among the two letters

parts.note: two ends of week, its first and last letters W and K
picking one or the other is expressed by the word for alternatives

explanation.surface: A shift worker is on duty every other weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'one of two weekends' as 'one of the two ends of week', W or K: put together, that phrase spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To work is to have a job and be employed by someone, a plain synonym.

parts.note: a machine that goes is working
to shy is to throw, as is to sling

explanation.surface: An idle youngster who avoids labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work-shy' reads as one adjective meaning lazy, but splits into two verbs, function and throw, set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A gosling is a baby goose, a young bird with wings.

clue.text: Having raised some little vandals, this might be contemplated

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised letters are read upwards, so backwards
some of the letters of the phrase little vandals are taken

explanation.surface: A parent of small troublemakers ends up reflecting on things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks LEVAN out of 'littLE VANdals' and 'raised' turns it upwards. Navel-gazing is the idiom for self-absorbed contemplation.
explanation.definitionFit: Navel-gazing means idle introspection, so the belly button is what a contemplative person proverbially stares at.

clue.text: Cavalryman that's died beside Gunner Milligan?

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died in genealogies
RA is the Royal Artillery, whose soldiers are gunners
Spike Milligan was a member of the Goons, the comedy team of radio's Goon Show

explanation.surface: A mounted soldier perishes alongside an artilleryman named Milligan.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan, the comedian, had served as a gunner in the Second World War, which feeds the surface. The Goon Show was a hit 1950s BBC radio comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Dragoons were mounted infantry, later cavalry regiments, so a dragoon is a horse soldier.

indicators.note: the relative eats, taking the round letter inside

parts.note: a gran is a grandmother
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O

explanation.surface: A complaint about grandma's meat choices at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' looks like meat, which 'eats' and 'duck' support; here it means a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is slang for a grievance, and a groan is a moan of complaint.

indicators.note: only the extreme letters, first and last, of seek are used

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: Hide and seek is a hugely popular children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide and seek' reads as the game, but 'Hide' is the definition and 'extremely' takes S and K from 'seek'.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's hide is its skin, a straight synonym.

indicators.note: the letters are taken from the words that follow, part of them

explanation.surface: Love is, at heart, a matter of good character.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'loVE Essentially'. Spelling a letter's name (VEE for V) is a standard crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A character can be a letter of the alphabet, and this is the spelled-out name of V.

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, flexibly, so the letters of Ken should bend into a new order

explanation.surface: Ken ought to provide some animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a verb but is an adverb from supple, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Elkhounds are a Norwegian dog breed, and dogs are an example of household pets.

definitions.meaning: to hit someone, informally to land one on them
to spot or see, as in British slang for catching sight of

explanation.surface: An announcement of industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike notice' reads as a walkout warning, but splits into two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Clock is British slang both for punching someone and for noticing them.

definitions.meaning: a profession here is a declaration, what a card dealer might say of their job

explanation.surface: Is being a croupier the best possible job?
explanation.walkthrough: 'profession' means a statement of what one does, not a career: a croupier professes 'I deal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ideal is perfect, the very best fit for a purpose.

definitions.meaning: a state without a monarch, here the large South Asian one
Ireland begins with I, whose NATO phonetic alphabet code word is wanted

explanation.surface: A national figure of the Irish Republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republic of Ireland' is a decoy phrase; the leading letter of Ireland is I, and India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: India has been a republic since 1950, and the NATO radio alphabet uses it as the word for the letter I.

clue.text: Short man finally shaved head for charity

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a king is one of the men, the pieces, in chess

indicators.note: only the end letter of shaved is used

parts.note: a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A short fellow has his head shaved for a good cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' is a chess piece, KING; 'Short' trims it to KIN. 'head' is a geographical one, as in Loch Ness's neighbouring promontories.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity in its older sense is goodwill and benevolence toward others, which is generosity of spirit.

indicators.note: the numeral gets into the other word, inside it

parts.note: to span a river is to cross it
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A competitor entering a cross-country race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross-country' reads as a race, but splits into 'cross' (SPAN) and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a nation of south-western Europe.

definitions.meaning: in Genesis the first man God created, arguably since evolution disputes it
Robert ... was an eighteenth-century Scottish architect

explanation.surface: Perhaps the earliest man to design buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arguably' hedges the biblical claim.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible names the first man, and the same surname belongs to the neoclassical architect Robert and his brothers.

indicators.note: the game sits within the country's code

parts.note: BD is the international vehicle code for Bangladesh
loo is an old card game

explanation.surface: Introduce someone to a card game played in Bangladesh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiate' looks like a verb meaning start; here it means to blood a newcomer.
explanation.definitionFit: To blood someone is to give them their first experience of something, initiating them, from the hunting custom.

indicators.note: cooked letters are worked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe: fruit prepared together with a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges GOT and BREAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Bergamot is a variety of pear, as well as the citrus fruit that flavours Earl Grey tea.

clue.text: Bottle setter consumed in the flipping toilet

indicators.note: the pronoun is taken inside the word for the toilet
flipped over, the letters run the other way; also a mild oath on the surface

parts.note: lav is short for lavatory
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: The setter knocked back a bottle in the wretched loo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed in' puts I inside LAV to make LAIV, and 'flipping', which reads as a curse, turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A vial is a small glass bottle for medicine or perfume.

indicators.note: treated roughly, the letters of the other entry are knocked about and rearranged

parts.note: points to the answer of 6 down, the belly button
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: About six spies have infiltrated a Spanish team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly 6' reads as 'about six' but rearranges the answer at 6 down to VALEN; 'in' is a link. 15 is SPAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Valencia CF is a leading football club from the Spanish city of the same name.

clue.text: Damn awful rain — bad language as a result

indicators.note: awful letters are a mess, so damn and rain are mixed together

explanation.surface: Someone curses the terrible weather, swearing because of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad language' looks like the definition but only 'language' is; 'awful' rearranges DAMN and RAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandarin is the chief spoken Chinese tongue, the most widely spoken first language in the world.

definitions.meaning: a flower, here a daffodil by its pet name
the cartoon character from Looney Tunes

explanation.surface: A mad mistake; take cover!
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' suggests a blunder and 'Duck!' a warning, but each is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Daffy means silly, is a nickname for the daffodil, and is the name of the Warner Bros cartoon duck.

definitions.meaning: a punctuation mark that halts a sentence partly
Colón is a port city on Panama's Caribbean coast

explanation.surface: A ship calls in at a harbour in the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' means a punctuation mark, not a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-dot mark is a punctuation stop, and Colón is the Panamanian port at the Atlantic end of the canal.

clue.text: Group of trees weighed down by first of easy peelers? On the contrary

indicators.note: says the stated relation is the other way about, so the letter from the top goes to the bottom instead
in a down entry, the piece doing the weighing sits on top of the other, pressing it down
only the opening letter of easy is used

parts.note: peelers is old British slang for police officers, after Sir Robert Peel; cops

explanation.surface: Trees bowed down beneath the first easy-peel fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, E sits on top of COPS (ECOPS); 'On the contrary' flips that, moving E to the foot. 'easy peelers' suggests small citrus fruit; peelers are police, after Sir Robert Peel.
explanation.definitionFit: A copse is a small wood or thicket, a cluster of trees.

clue.text: Port in Germany agreed, following article

parts.note: ja is German for yes
ff is the abbreviation for following pages
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A harbour in Germany agreed to follow some clause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following article' tempts a reading of 'after A', but FF is the reference-book abbreviation, followed by A in answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaffa is an ancient port on the coast of Israel, now part of Tel Aviv.

clue.text: Taking tops of jars off, leave this jar

indicators.note: in a down entry the tops are the first letters of each word that follows

explanation.surface: Removing the lids from jars, abandon this container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking tops of' picks the first letters of 'jars off leave this'.
explanation.definitionFit: To jar is to jolt, to shake with a sudden bump.

clue.text: Model, short of time, gets soft drink

indicators.note: lacking the letter, so it is removed

parts.note: to sit is to model for an artist
p, piano, is the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: A model pressed for time grabs a soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soft drink' reads as one item, but 'soft' gives P and 'drink' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To sip is to drink in small mouthfuls.

clue.text: MAD magazine no longer in print

definitions.meaning: a British men's weekly magazine that closed in 2014

explanation.surface: MAD, the satirical magazine, has stopped publishing.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitals make 'MAD' look like the US humour magazine; it is just the adjective. Nuts was a UK lads' mag.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is slang for insane, and was also the title of a defunct British weekly.

indicators.note: the letter is put to use inside the other word

parts.note: Bristols is rhyming slang for breasts (Bristol City, titty), so one Bristol is a tit
L, left, is one side

explanation.surface: A football ground's touchline in the city of Bristol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bristol' looks like the English city; it is Cockney rhyming slang, Bristol City for titty. 'Pitch side' reads as a touchline.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch is to lean or slope, so pitch and tilt are synonyms for an incline.

clue.text: Have fun with me: cause confusion and mischief abroad

parts.note: to play is to enjoy oneself
the setter of this puzzle signs as Hob

explanation.surface: An invitation to enjoy the setter's company while stirring up trouble abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'me' means the setter, Hob. 'abroad' works as a link: playing hob means going about causing mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: Play hob is an idiom for creating havoc; a hob is a mischievous sprite like a hobgoblin.

clue.text: City in 15 getting two points against town in France

parts.note: S and E are two compass points, south and east
ville is French for town

explanation.surface: A Spanish city scores two points against a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is SPAIN; 'getting' and 'against' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Seville is the capital of Andalusia in southern Spain.
